bib.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
bib.venue: UIST '23 (36th ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed for lineage only.

question: How can an LLM-based agent architecture produce believable individual and emergent social behavior over long horizons in an interactive sandbox?
hypothesis: Observation, planning and reflection over a natural-language memory stream are each needed for believable behavior; removing any should reduce believability.
contributions: Generative agents, believable simulacra of human behavior that are dynamically conditioned on agents' changing experiences and environment.
A novel architecture (memory stream, retrieval, reflection, planning) letting agents remember, retrieve, reflect, interact and plan.
Two evaluations, a controlled evaluation and an end-to-end evaluation, establishing causal effects of the architecture's components and identifying breakdowns.
Discussion of opportunities and ethical and societal risks of generative agents.

method.summary: A memory stream of natural-language records (observations, reflections, plans) is retrieved by a weighted sum of recency, importance and relevance and fed to gpt3.5-turbo, which also generates reflections, daily plans, reactions and dialogue. 25 agents live in a Phaser-based sandbox (Smallville) for two game days; believability is ranked by 100 human raters against ablations and a crowdworker baseline.
method.task: Believable agent behavior simulation (memory retrieval, reflection, planning, reaction, dialogue)

datasets.name: Smallville agent seed descriptions
datasets.size: 25 agents, one paragraph each (semicolon-delimited phrases become initial memories)
datasets.preprocessing: each semicolon-delimited phrase entered as an initial memory

datasets.name: Interview questions
datasets.split: one random question per category shown to each rater

models.name: gpt3.5-turbo (ChatGPT)
models.architecture: LLM, used via API for generation, importance rating, embeddings

other.note: GPT-4 API was invitation-only at time of writing

inference.samples: One 2-day simulation of 25 agents; interviews taken at end of the 2 game days; each of 100 raters ranked responses to one random question per category
inference.prompting: Zero-shot natural-language prompts for importance rating, reflection questions, insights, daily plan, reaction, dialogue, location choice (see prompts).
inference.retrieval: Score = alpha_recency*recency + alpha_importance*importance + alpha_relevance*relevance, each min-max scaled to [0,1], all alphas 1; top-ranked memories that fit the context window go into the prompt.

parameters.recency_decay: 0.995 exponential decay per sandbox game hour since the memory was last retrieved
parameters.relevance: cosine similarity of LLM embeddings of memory and query
parameters.reflection_threshold: 150 (sum of importance scores of latest events)
parameters.reflection_context: 100 most recent memory records; 3 salient questions; 5 insights
parameters.plan_granularity: 5-8 chunks per day, then hour-long, then 5-15 minute chunks
parameters.real_to_game_time: one second real time is one minute game time

other.cost: thousands of dollars in token credits and multiple days for 25 agents over two days

metrics.name: TrueSkill rating (mu, sigma)
metrics.definition: Computed from 100 participants' rankings of 5 conditions by believability

metrics.name: Information diffusion
metrics.definition: Percentage of the 25 agents answering yes to knowing the party / the mayoral candidacy, verified against memory stream

metrics.name: Party attendance
metrics.definition: Number of invited agents who showed up

baselines: no observation, no reflection, no planning (prior art)
eval.protocol: Within-subjects; 100 Prolific raters (US, fluent English, >18, $15.00/hour, ~30 min) ranked 5 conditions; ablations given equivalent access to all memories accrued up to interview time (no re-simulation). Single simulation, no repeated runs reported. Crowdworker baseline: one worker per agent (25); four sets re-generated.

prompts.text:
On the scale of 1 to 10, where 1 is purely mundane (e.g., brushing teeth, making bed) and 10 is extremely poignant (e.g., a break up, college acceptance), rate the likely poignancy of the following piece of memory.
Memory: buying groceries at The Willows Market and Pharmacy
Rating: <fill in>
Given only the information above, what are 3 most salient high-level questions we can answer about the subjects in the statements?
What 5 high-level insights can you infer from the above statements? (example format: insight (because of 1, 5, 3))
Should John react to the observation, and if so, what would be an appropriate reaction?

* Prefer to stay in the current area if the activity can be done there.
Eddy Lin is planning to take a short walk around his workspace. Which area should Eddy Lin go to?

results.claim: The full architecture is the most believable of five conditions.
results.setup: 100 Prolific raters ranking 5 conditions; agents sampled at end of 2-game-day simulation; gpt3.5-turbo; ablations given all accrued memories
results.quote: the full generative agent architecture produced the most believable behavior (𝜇= 29.89; 𝜎= 0.72)

results.claim: No-reflection ablation (observations and plans) ranks next.
results.quote: the ablated architecture with no access to reflection was the next best (𝜇= 26.88; 𝜎= 0.69)

results.claim: No reflection and no planning (observations only) scored lower.
results.quote: followed by no access to reflection or planning (𝜇= 25.64; 𝜎= 0.68)

results.claim: Human crowdworker-authored responses scored below three of the architectures.
results.setup: one crowdworker per agent, role-playing after watching a replay; not maximal human performance

results.claim: The fully ablated condition (prior-art style) is worst.
Effect size of full architecture over the prior-art condition.
results.setup: TrueSkill skill modelled as N(mu, sigma^2)
results.quote: produces a standardized effect size of 𝑑= 8.16, or eight standard deviations

results.setup: raw ranks; all pairwise Dunn differences p<0.001 except crowdworker vs fully ablated

results.claim: Knowledge of Sam's candidacy spread from 1 to 8 of 25 agents.
results.setup: two game days, no user intervention, interview at end, checked against memory stream

results.claim: Knowledge of the party spread from 1 to 13 of 25 agents.
Network density rose over two days.
results.quote: the network density increasing from 0.167 to 0.74

results.claim: Hallucinated awareness responses were a small share.
Only five of twelve invited agents attended the party.
results.setup: Valentine's Day party at Hobbs Cafe; 3 of 7 absentees cited conflicts, 4 expressed interest but did not plan to come
results.quote: five out of the twelve invited agents showed up at Hobbs cafe to join the party

results.claim: Reflection fired roughly two or three times a day at threshold 150.
results.setup: implementation setting; agents reflected roughly two or three times a day
results.note: Frequency stated in text as 'roughly two or three times a day' (game days).

results.claim: Cost of the simulation was high.
results.setup: 25 agents, two game days, gpt3.5-turbo; described as thousands of dollars in token credits and multiple days, no exact figure

limits: Evaluation covers a short timescale (two game days) and a single simulation with no repeated runs.
Ablations were given all memories accrued by the full architecture rather than re-simulated; authors say this likely underestimates true differences.
Crowdworker baseline does not represent maximal human performance.
Most common errors: failed retrieval, embellished memories, overly formal speech inherited from instruction tuning; agents also chose atypical locations as memory/location knowledge grew.
Robustness (prompt hacking, memory hacking, hallucination) untested; cost is thousands of dollars of tokens for 25 agents over two days.
Built on gpt3.5-turbo; weights/hyperparameters (alphas) not varied; temperature and decoding not stated.
